summary:
EarthSignal is an integrated agricultural monitoring and food-production research platform developed to support agricultural resilience on Earth and explore research relevant to future food production in space.

The platform brings together three connected workspaces: the Farmer Dashboard, Research Workspace, and Space Crop Research. The Farmer Dashboard combines field soil-moisture readings from an ESP32-based SoilSense device with weather information to help users monitor growing conditions. The Research Workspace uses NASA POWER environmental data to explore historical rainfall and air-temperature patterns across different locations. Space Crop Research enables users to create controlled growing experiments, record habitat conditions, track water use and document crop growth.

By connecting field monitoring, environmental research and controlled crop experiments, EarthSignal makes agricultural information more accessible while developing methods relevant to resource-efficient food production. Its space research direction draws on NASA's plant-growth research aboard the International Space Station without claiming to reproduce microgravity conditions.
details:
What EarthSignal does

EarthSignal is built around three connected workspaces within one integrated platform.

1. Farmer Dashboard

The Farmer Dashboard allows users to register farm details, monitor soil-moisture readings from an ESP32-based SoilSense device, and view current weather conditions, recent weather records and forecasts through Open-Meteo. It also provides monitoring alerts and contextual information to help farmers understand field conditions.

We are extending this workspace with SMS alerts, a farmer-support chatbot and local-language access to make agricultural information more accessible, particularly for farmers who may have limited internet access.

2. Research Workspace

The Research Workspace uses NASA POWER data to explore historical rainfall and air-temperature patterns across selected locations. Users can search for locations, load environmental records, compare selected areas and examine historical trends. These records provide regional environmental context for agricultural research rather than claiming to represent measurements taken directly at every farm.

3. Space Crop Research

Space Crop Research allows users to create controlled plant-growing experiments, define comparison groups, record environmental conditions, document crop growth and track water supplied and harvested biomass. It also provides a way to examine published NASA plant-growth research aboard the International Space Station.

The workspace connects terrestrial crop experiments with research questions about growing food under limited environmental and resource conditions in space. Earth-based experiments are not presented as microgravity simulations.

How the system works

NASA POWER provides historical environmental data to the Research Workspace. Open-Meteo supplies weather information to the Farmer Dashboard. The ESP32 SoilSense device reads soil moisture through an analogue sensor and sends its readings to the EarthSignal backend through a sensor API.

The backend validates incoming readings and stores them in an SQLite database. The web application retrieves and presents the information through interactive charts and dashboards. Users can also enter controlled experiment observations and habitat measurements.

Technology used

  • Python and FastAPI for the backend and API.
  • JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the web application.
  • C++ using the Arduino framework for ESP32 firmware.
  • SQLite for data storage.
  • Chart.js for data visualisation.
  • NASA POWER for historical environmental data.
  • Open-Meteo for weather information.
  • ESP32 and a soil-moisture probe for physical field monitoring.

Benefits and intended impact

EarthSignal brings together field monitoring, environmental data analysis and controlled crop research in one platform. It is intended to support better access to agricultural information, help researchers investigate environmental conditions affecting plant growth, and develop practical approaches to monitoring water and growing resources.

Its longer-term research direction explores how methods developed for terrestrial crop monitoring and controlled growing experiments can contribute to research into food production for future space missions.

Creative approach

The project connects three areas that are often treated separately: practical farm monitoring, location-based environmental research and controlled plant-growth experiments with a space-food research direction. This creates a shared platform where agricultural observations and research findings can inform further experiments.

The team has considered data reliability, sensor calibration, differences between regional environmental estimates and field measurements, resource tracking, accessibility and the scientific limitations of comparing Earth-based experiments with space-grown crops.
